business_problem: General-purpose LLMs can produce subtle but consequential errors in legal and compliance work, where professionals need trustworthy, citation-backed analysis across very large document sets.
solution_summary: Thomson Reuters built Thomson as a proprietary large language model for legal and compliance work, then deployed it inside CoCounsel rather than exposing the model as a standalone end-user product. The source says Thomson was built on Thomson Reuters proprietary legal content, specifically Westlaw and Practical Law, plus input from human legal experts, giving the model domain depth beyond general-purpose AI. In production, CoCounsel serves as the agentic workspace and application layer, and its Tabular Analysis feature orchestrates the workflow: users define up to 100 questions and submit up to 10,000 documents, then CoCounsel calls Thomson to extract structured answers with linked citations. The page does not name a separate storage platform, but it explicitly identifies Westlaw and Practical Law as the authoritative content foundation and says Thomson is governed through enterprise-grade frameworks for transparency, traceability, verifiability, structured evaluation, and expert validation.

data_flow: Authoritative legal content from Westlaw and Practical Law, together with Thomson Reuters expert input, is used to build and refine Thomson. In production, legal professionals use CoCounsel's Tabular Analysis to submit up to 10,000 documents and up to 100 questions. CoCounsel calls Thomson to analyze the corpus and return structured, citation-linked answers that attorneys can review and rely on.
